conditions.name: Hypertension
conditions.overview: Study adult blood pressure classification, confirmation and risk-guided medication decisions under the 2025 US recommendations.

sources.title: Top Things to Know: 2025 High Blood Pressure (BP) Guideline
sources.locator: Items 4, 6–10; nonpregnant adult blood pressure classification and treatment

sources.title: New High Blood Pressure Guideline Emphasizes Prevention, Early Treatment to Reduce CVD Risk
sources.locator: Blood pressure criteria; home monitoring; Tailored approaches to medication

sections.title: Classify and confirm
sections.text: Stage 1 is systolic 130–139 or diastolic 80–89 mm Hg; stage 2 is systolic ≥140 or diastolic ≥90. Confirm with standardized measurements and appropriate home monitoring.

sections.title: Risk-guided treatment
sections.text: Medication plus lifestyle change is recommended at ≥140/90, or at ≥130/80 with relevant comorbidities or PREVENT 10-year cardiovascular risk ≥7.5%. Lower-risk persistent hypertension after 3–6 months of lifestyle change also warrants medication.

sections.title: Initial therapy and goals
sections.text: Usual treatment goal is <130/80 with individual exceptions. Stage 2 favors two first-line drugs of different classes; examples include an ARB and long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old has confirmed average BP 136/84 mm Hg and PREVENT 10-year cardiovascular risk 9%, without pregnancy or treatment contraindications. Which approach best follows the 2025 guideline?

choices.text: Lifestyle change plus antihypertensive medication
Lifestyle change only indefinitely
Wait until BP reaches 160/100
Use a smartwatch as the only confirmation
Avoid home BP monitoring

questions.explanation: At ≥130/80 with PREVENT risk ≥7.5%, medication accompanies lifestyle intervention.

distractorExplanations.B: Risk is above the treatment threshold.
distractorExplanations.C: That delays indicated treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Cuffless devices lack adequate reliability.
distractorExplanations.E: Home monitoring supports management.

questions.learningObjective: Apply PREVENT risk to stage 1 hypertension treatment.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has newly confirmed BP 152/96 mm Hg and no compelling drug-specific indication. Which initial regimen best matches the guideline preference?

choices.text: Two ARBs
An ARB plus a long-acting dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker
No medication for one year
A short-acting drug only as needed
Two thiazide-type diuretics

questions.explanation: Stage 2 favors two first-line classes, preferably as a single combination pill.

distractorExplanations.A: These are the same class.
distractorExplanations.C: Persistent stage 2 warrants medication.
distractorExplanations.D: As-needed dosing is not the preferred initial plan.
distractorExplanations.E: These belong to the same class rather than two different first-line classes.

questions.learningObjective: Select a two-class initial regimen for stage 2 hypertension.

conditions.name: Hypertensive emergency
conditions.overview: Distinguish severe asymptomatic blood pressure elevation from a suspected hypertensive emergency.

sources.title: When To Call 911 About High Blood Pressure
sources.locator: Severe hypertension; Hypertensive emergency; emergency symptoms

sources.title: Top Things to Know: 2025 High Blood Pressure (BP) Guideline
sources.locator: Items 4, 6–10; nonpregnant adult blood pressure classification and treatment

sections.title: Recognize danger
sections.text: Marked BP elevation with new chest pain, dyspnea, weakness, visual change or difficulty speaking raises concern for acute organ injury and warrants emergency evaluation.

sections.title: Do not use BP alone
sections.text: A BP above 180/120 without acute organ-damage evidence is severe hypertension, not automatically a hypertensive emergency. Evaluate promptly and distinguish symptoms and examination findings.

sections.title: Match disposition to injury
sections.text: Suspected hypertensive emergency requires immediate emergency care. The 2025 guideline instead favors timely oral-treatment initiation or intensification for nonpregnant severe hypertension without acute organ damage.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old at a clinic has BP 214/128 mm Hg, new dyspnea and chest pressure. What is the best immediate disposition?

choices.text: Routine follow-up in three months
Home rest until symptoms stop
Activate emergency services for urgent evaluation
Only repeat BP tomorrow
Begin an exercise session

questions.explanation: Severe BP with new chest symptoms or dyspnea requires emergency evaluation.

distractorExplanations.A: New symptoms make routine delay unsafe.
distractorExplanations.B: Waiting could miss acute organ injury.
distractorExplanations.D: A next-day check delays evaluation.
distractorExplanations.E: Exercise does not address this emergency.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize symptoms requiring emergency escalation.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has repeat BP 188/124 mm Hg after stopping prescribed medication. Assessment finds no symptoms or evidence of acute organ damage. Which plan best fits the 2025 recommendation?

choices.text: Automatically label hypertensive emergency from the number alone
Ignore the result because symptoms are absent
Exercise to rapidly lower BP before evaluation
Timely reinstitution or intensification of oral therapy with follow-up
Delay all treatment six months

questions.explanation: Severe hypertension without acute organ damage calls for timely oral management rather than assuming an emergency solely from BP.

distractorExplanations.A: Organ injury distinguishes the emergency.
distractorExplanations.B: Severe hypertension still needs management.
distractorExplanations.C: This is not a substitute for evaluation.
distractorExplanations.E: That is not timely treatment.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish severe asymptomatic hypertension from emergency.

conditions.name: Dyslipidemia
conditions.overview: Study contemporary lipid risk assessment and the 2026 US guideline update.

sources.title: Top Things to Know: Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
sources.locator: Items 2, 6 and 7: PREVENT-ASCVD, lipoprotein(a), selective coronary calcium

sources.title: 2026 Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
sources.locator: Replacement of 2018 cholesterol guideline; key updates

sections.title: Use current risk assessment
sections.text: The 2026 guideline uses PREVENT-ASCVD rather than the older Pooled Cohort Equations for primary prevention risk assessment in adults aged 30–79.

sections.title: Lipoprotein(a)
sections.text: Measure Lp(a) at least once to identify inherited risk that a conventional lipid panel may not reveal; elevated values support more intensive risk-factor management.

sections.title: Personalize prevention
sections.text: The 2026 guideline restores risk-specific LDL-C/non-HDL-C goals and expands selective CAC assessment when additional risk classification would affect treatment. It replaces the 2018 cholesterol guideline.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old without known ASCVD needs an initial cardiovascular risk estimate to discuss lipid-lowering therapy. Which tool does the 2026 guideline prefer?

choices.text: Wells score
CHA2DS2-VASc
CURB-65
The older Pooled Cohort Equations as the preferred current tool
PREVENT-ASCVD

questions.explanation: PREVENT-ASCVD is the recommended contemporary primary-prevention framework.

distractorExplanations.A: Wells evaluates a different clinical problem.
distractorExplanations.B: CHA2DS2-VASc addresses AF stroke risk.
distractorExplanations.C: CURB-65 addresses a different illness.
distractorExplanations.D: The guideline moved from PCE to PREVENT-ASCVD.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the current lipid primary-prevention risk tool.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old with a strong family history of premature ASCVD has never had Lp(a) measured. Which action best follows the 2026 guideline?

choices.text: Measure Lp(a) at least once
Avoid testing because LDL-C is normal
Measure Lp(a) only after a heart attack
Replace all lipid testing with urinalysis
Assume lifestyle excludes inherited risk

questions.explanation: At least one Lp(a) measurement can reveal risk beyond the conventional lipid panel.

distractorExplanations.B: LDL-C does not exclude elevated Lp(a).
distractorExplanations.C: Waiting for an event misses risk assessment.
distractorExplanations.D: Urinalysis does not measure this biomarker.
distractorExplanations.E: Healthy habits do not exclude inherited risk.

questions.learningObjective: Use Lp(a) testing in lifelong lipid risk assessment.

conditions.overview: Study diagnostic confirmation and comorbidity-directed therapy using federal clinical guidance.

sources.title: Diabetes & Prediabetes Tests

sources.locator: A1C test; confirmation and differing test results

sources.title: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Provider Summary
sources.organization: Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense
sources.locator: Recommendation 2 (prediabetes), recommendations 21–22 (heart failure and CKD), Table 3 metformin; May 2023 printed edition

sections.title: Confirm diagnosis
sections.text: Laboratory A1C ≥6.5% meets a diabetes threshold. In an asymptomatic person, confirm the abnormal finding with repeat diagnostic testing rather than relying on one result.

sections.title: Treat beyond A1C
sections.text: VA/DoD recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes with heart failure to reduce heart-failure hospitalization, and an agent with proven renal benefit when CKD is present.

sections.title: Medication safety
sections.text: Medication selection must consider kidney function. The VA/DoD pharmacotherapy table lists metformin as contraindicated below eGFR 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; do not equate glycemic efficacy with suitability.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic adult has a first laboratory A1C of 6.7%. No prior glucose results are available. What is the best next diagnostic step?

choices.text: Declare that A1C can never diagnose diabetes
Repeat diagnostic testing to confirm diabetes
Start lifelong insulin without confirmation
Classify the result as normal
Use a urine glucose dipstick as the only confirmation

questions.explanation: A1C meets the diabetes threshold, but an asymptomatic first abnormal result needs confirmation.

distractorExplanations.A: A1C is an accepted diagnostic test.
distractorExplanations.C: Confirmation is the issue in this vignette.
distractorExplanations.D: 6.7% exceeds the threshold.
distractorExplanations.E: Urine glucose is not the indicated confirmation.

questions.learningObjective: Confirm an asymptomatic diabetes-range A1C.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with type 2 diabetes and stable heart failure has eGFR 65 and no contraindication to the choices. Which drug class is specifically recommended to reduce heart-failure admissions?

choices.text: Sulfonylurea
Meglitinide
SGLT2 inhibitor
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
Insulin solely for its claimed heart-failure prevention effect

questions.explanation: VA/DoD recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for this heart-failure outcome.

distractorExplanations.A: It is not the class specified for this outcome.
distractorExplanations.B: It is not the class specified for this outcome.
distractorExplanations.D: It is not the class specified for this outcome.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated prevention claim does not identify the recommended class.

questions.learningObjective: Choose diabetes therapy with established heart-failure benefit.

conditions.name: Prediabetes
conditions.overview: Study recognition, progression surveillance and diabetes prevention.

sources.title: Insulin Resistance & Prediabetes
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: Blood tests; annual diabetes testing; Managing your weight; Medicines

sources.title: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: Provider Summary
sources.organization: Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense
sources.locator: Recommendation 2 (prediabetes), recommendations 21–22 (heart failure and CKD), Table 3 metformin; May 2023 printed edition

sections.title: Identify prediabetes
sections.text: A1C 5.7–6.4%, fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL, or two-hour OGTT glucose 140–199 mg/dL falls in the prediabetes range.

sections.title: Reduce progression risk
sections.text: A structured lifestyle program addressing activity and weight can delay diabetes. NIH DPP data support a 5–7% initial weight-loss target when excess weight is present.

sections.title: Follow progression
sections.text: NIDDK advises annual type 2 diabetes testing after prediabetes is identified. VA/DoD also supports lifestyle changes and selected medication prevention for higher-risk adults.

questions.stem: An adult has A1C 6.1% confirmed on repeat testing and no diabetes symptoms. Which classification best fits?

choices.text: Normal glycemia
Type 1 diabetes established by A1C alone
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Prediabetes
Type 2 diabetes established by this value

questions.explanation: 6.1% is within the prediabetes A1C range of 5.7–6.4%.

distractorExplanations.A: The value is above the normal range.
distractorExplanations.B: This result does not establish type 1 diabetes.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not demonstrate ketoacidosis.
distractorExplanations.E: It is below the diabetes A1C threshold.

questions.learningObjective: Classify an A1C in the prediabetes range.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old with obesity and newly identified prediabetes begins a prevention program. Which paired plan is best supported?

choices.text: No retesting until symptoms develop
Avoid physical activity and check once in ten years
Treat all such patients with insulin
Rely on urine glucose alone each decade
Weight-loss/activity support and annual diabetes testing

questions.explanation: Weight/activity intervention reduces progression risk; annual testing monitors for diabetes.

distractorExplanations.A: Waiting for symptoms misses progression.
distractorExplanations.B: That omits useful prevention and surveillance.
distractorExplanations.C: Insulin is not the specified prevention approach.
distractorExplanations.D: This is not the recommended surveillance.

questions.learningObjective: Pair diabetes prevention with appropriate surveillance.

conditions.name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
conditions.overview: Study insulin dependence, adult presentations and prevention of metabolic emergencies.

sources.title: Type 1 Diabetes
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: Who is more likely to develop type 1 diabetes?; How can I manage type 1 diabetes?; insulin and autoantibodies

sources.title: High Risk for Hypoglycemia Guideline Resources
sources.locator: Recommendations 1, 9 and 10; fingerstick confirmation remarks

sections.title: Age does not exclude type 1
sections.text: Type 1 diabetes may appear in adulthood. Classification can require autoantibody testing; a glucose diagnostic test alone does not determine diabetes type.

sections.title: Insulin is essential
sections.text: Established type 1 diabetes requires insulin. Delivery can use injections, pens or pumps alongside glucose monitoring and a tailored education plan.

sections.title: Recognize ketoacidosis risk
sections.text: Insulin deficiency increases ketone production and DKA risk, particularly during infection or other physiological stress. Review warning symptoms and emergency plans.

sections.title: Glucose monitoring recommendation
sections.text: Endocrine Society guidance favors CGM for type 1 diabetes treated with multiple daily injections. Retain fingerstick testing to confirm discordant symptoms or readings.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old with established autoimmune type 1 diabetes asks which treatment is indispensable even when diet is carefully managed. Which is the best answer?

choices.text: Insulin
A carbohydrate-free diet alone
An herbal supplement alone
Exercise alone
A statin as the sole diabetes drug

questions.explanation: Insulin is essential in established type 1 diabetes.

distractorExplanations.B: Diet does not replace missing insulin.
distractorExplanations.C: A supplement does not replace insulin.
distractorExplanations.D: Activity does not replace insulin.
distractorExplanations.E: A statin does not replace insulin.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the indispensable treatment for type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: An adult with type 1 diabetes uses multiple daily insulin injections and has recurring glucose fluctuations. Which monitoring approach best matches Endocrine Society guidance?

choices.text: Fingerstick monitoring is always preferred over CGM
Use CGM while retaining fingerstick confirmation when needed
Stop monitoring once insulin is prescribed
Use symptoms alone without glucose measurements
Treat every discordant sensor reading without confirmation

questions.explanation: CGM is recommended with multiple daily injections; fingerstick confirmation remains available for discordant symptoms or sensor limitations.

distractorExplanations.A: The recommendation favors CGM.
distractorExplanations.C: Insulin does not eliminate monitoring needs.
distractorExplanations.D: Symptoms alone do not provide glucose measurements.
distractorExplanations.E: Discordant readings may require confirmation.

questions.learningObjective: Apply CGM guidance while recognizing the need for confirmatory fingerstick testing.

conditions.name: Hypoglycemia
conditions.overview: Study rapid recognition and treatment of medication-associated low blood glucose.

sources.title: Low Blood Glucose (Hypoglycemia)
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: Causes; How do I treat low blood glucose?; severe low blood glucose and glucagon

sources.title: High Risk for Hypoglycemia Guideline Resources
sources.locator: Recommendations 1, 9 and 10; fingerstick confirmation remarks

sections.title: Identify a low value
sections.text: For many adults with diabetes, glucose <70 mg/dL is low. Insulin and insulin-secretagogue drugs, missed meals, increased activity and alcohol can contribute.

sections.title: Treat when swallowing is safe
sections.text: An alert person able to swallow can take 15–20 g of fast carbohydrate or glucose; recheck after 15 minutes and repeat if still low.

sections.title: Severe episodes need rescue
sections.text: If a person cannot self-treat safely, glucagon can be given by a trained helper and emergency help is required. Prevention includes reviewing medications and eating/activity patterns.

sections.title: Prevent recurrent severe episodes
sections.text: Insulin-treated patients benefit from structured hypoglycemia education. For outpatient severe episodes, Endocrine Society guidance favors ready-to-use glucagon over preparations requiring mixing.

questions.stem: An insulin-treated adult is awake, can swallow and has glucose 58 mg/dL after missing lunch. What is the best immediate action?

choices.text: Give extra insulin
Wait until the next scheduled visit
Provide 15–20 g fast carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes
Take only plain water
Begin vigorous exercise

questions.explanation: Safe oral glucose/carbohydrate with prompt reassessment treats this episode.

distractorExplanations.A: Extra insulin does not correct a low value.
distractorExplanations.B: Treatment should not be delayed.
distractorExplanations.D: Water does not supply glucose.
distractorExplanations.E: Activity may further lower glucose.

questions.learningObjective: Treat hypoglycemia when oral intake is safe.

questions.stem: A family member finds an insulin-treated adult unable to cooperate or swallow safely; a glucose check is very low. A prescribed glucagon kit is available and the helper is trained. Which response is best?

choices.text: Force solid food into the mouth
Wait for spontaneous awakening
Give a corrective insulin dose
Give glucagon and activate emergency help
Offer diet soda only

questions.explanation: Glucagon rescue and emergency assistance are appropriate when self-treatment is unsafe.

distractorExplanations.A: Unsafe swallowing rules out this option.
distractorExplanations.B: Severe hypoglycemia needs rescue.
distractorExplanations.C: Insulin is not rescue for a low glucose.
distractorExplanations.E: Diet soda does not supply rescue glucose.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize when glucagon and emergency help are needed.

conditions.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis
conditions.overview: Study DKA warning features and emergency treatment principles; this module does not provide a dosing protocol.

sources.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Signs and symptoms; Test for ketones; High ketones? Call 911; Treatment

sources.title: The Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Adults
sources.organization: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care
sources.edition: Revised March 2023; United Kingdom; CC BY-NC 4.0
sources.locator: Page 3 copyright; page 9 pathway; pages 20–21 potassium and hypoglycemia complications

sections.title: Recognize the syndrome
sections.text: Insulin deficiency promotes ketone production. Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing and fruity breath in a person with diabetes suggest DKA.

sections.title: Escalate promptly
sections.text: High ketones with DKA symptoms require emergency evaluation; inability to keep fluids down or difficulty breathing should not be managed as routine outpatient hyperglycemia.

sections.title: Understand treatment components
sections.text: Emergency treatment addresses fluid loss, electrolytes, insulin deficiency and the precipitating illness. A glucose value alone does not replace clinical assessment.

sections.title: Supplementary UK inpatient safety guidance
sections.text: UK JBDS guidance stresses repeated glucose, ketone and potassium assessment during treatment to avoid hypoglycemia and potassium complications. This supplement does not replace US inpatient protocols.

questions.stem: An adult with diabetes has vomiting, fruity breath, fast deep breathing and high urine ketones. Which action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Wait one week for a routine appointment
Only restrict carbohydrates at home
Begin vigorous exercise
Treat as isolated anxiety without assessment
Emergency evaluation now

questions.explanation: The combination is concerning for DKA and requires immediate emergency evaluation.

distractorExplanations.A: The warning features require prompt care.
distractorExplanations.B: Diet does not address the emergency.
distractorExplanations.C: Exercise is not the appropriate disposition.
distractorExplanations.D: The metabolic features need evaluation.

questions.learningObjective: Identify DKA warning features requiring emergency care.

questions.stem: A hospitalized patient has confirmed DKA triggered by an infection. Which treatment bundle addresses the principal problems?

choices.text: Fluid and electrolyte management, insulin and treatment of the trigger
Insulin alone without reassessing hydration or electrolytes
Antibiotics alone
A statin and no metabolic treatment
Discharge solely because thirst briefly improves

questions.explanation: DKA care addresses volume, electrolytes, insulin deficiency and its trigger.

distractorExplanations.B: That omits other key treatment components.
distractorExplanations.C: Infection treatment does not replace metabolic treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: This does not address DKA.
distractorExplanations.E: Symptom improvement alone does not establish resolution.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the components of DKA treatment without memorizing an unsafe isolated dose.

conditions.name: Hypothyroidism
conditions.overview: Study biochemical interpretation, replacement therapy and monitoring.

sources.title: Adult Hypothyroidism
sources.locator: How is hypothyroidism diagnosed?; How is hypothyroidism treated?; Follow-up

sources.title: New Hypothyroidism Treatment Guidelines from American Thyroid Association Published in Thyroid Journal
sources.locator: Guideline announcement conclusion on levothyroxine standard therapy; not full guideline text

sections.title: Interpret TSH and free T4
sections.text: High TSH with low free T4 supports primary hypothyroidism. Pituitary disease can make TSH misleading, so interpret it with free T4 and clinical context.

sections.title: Replace missing hormone
sections.text: Levothyroxine is the standard hormone replacement; ATA recommendations do not establish routine superiority of alternative preparations over levothyroxine.

sections.title: Allow time for reassessment
sections.text: ATA patient guidance advises blood testing 6–8 weeks after starting or changing a hormone dose; pregnancy and other factors may require closer monitoring.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old has fatigue, elevated TSH and low free T4, with no pituitary history. Which treatment best targets the hormonal deficit?

choices.text: Methimazole
Levothyroxine
Radioactive iodine
Propylthiouracil
A beta blocker as replacement hormone

questions.explanation: This pattern supports primary hypothyroidism, for which levothyroxine replaces deficient hormone.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not replace deficient hormone.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not replace deficient hormone.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not replace deficient hormone.
distractorExplanations.E: A beta blocker is not thyroid hormone.

questions.learningObjective: Match primary hypothyroidism to hormone replacement.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has a levothyroxine dose adjustment without urgent complications. When does ATA patient guidance recommend routine repeat blood testing?

choices.text: The next day
Only if a nodule develops
After 6–8 weeks
After five years
Never after a dose change

questions.explanation: The usual reassessment interval after a dose change is 6–8 weeks.

distractorExplanations.A: That is earlier than the stated routine interval.
distractorExplanations.B: Nodules are not required to monitor replacement.
distractorExplanations.D: That delays reassessment excessively.
distractorExplanations.E: Dose changes require follow-up testing.

questions.learningObjective: Plan routine monitoring after thyroid hormone adjustment.

conditions.name: Hyperthyroidism
conditions.overview: Study cause-specific therapy and antithyroid-drug safety.

sources.title: Hyperthyroidism
sources.locator: How is hyperthyroidism diagnosed?; Beta blockers; Antithyroid drugs; fever/sore throat precautions; thyroiditis

sources.title: American Thyroid Association Task Force Updates Treatment Guidelines for Hyperthyroidism
sources.edition: Clinical Thyroidology for the Public, November 2016; summary of 2016 ATA guideline
sources.locator: Retained recommendations: cause-specific treatment and active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease

sections.title: Confirm and determine cause
sections.text: Hyperthyroidism generally shows low TSH with high T4 and/or T3. Graves disease, autonomous nodules and thyroiditis require different management.

sections.title: Match treatment to mechanism
sections.text: Beta blockers can reduce adrenergic symptoms. Antithyroid drugs inhibit new hormone synthesis and are ineffective for thyroiditis-related leakage of stored hormone.

sections.title: Recognize a drug emergency
sections.text: Fever or severe sore throat during methimazole or PTU treatment requires urgent assessment and CBC; withhold further doses pending clearance because agranulocytosis is possible.

sections.title: Recognize a treatment-selection qualifier
sections.text: ATA guidance favors antithyroid medication or surgery over radioactive iodine for active moderate-to-severe or sight-threatening Graves eye disease; decisions remain individualized.

questions.stem: A patient with confirmed thyroiditis has transient thyrotoxicosis and bothersome palpitations. There is no beta-blocker contraindication. Which option best addresses symptoms without targeting new hormone synthesis?

choices.text: Methimazole as mandatory definitive therapy
Levothyroxine
Radioactive iodine for every thyroiditis episode
A beta blocker
Ignore symptomatic tachycardia

questions.explanation: Beta blockers address symptoms; antithyroid drugs do not treat hormone leakage from thyroiditis.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not treat this mechanism.
distractorExplanations.B: It supplies thyroid hormone.
distractorExplanations.C: Radioactive iodine is not effective for thyroiditis.
distractorExplanations.E: Symptoms still merit assessment and management.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish thyroiditis from hormone-overproduction disorders.

questions.stem: An adult taking methimazole for Graves disease develops fever and severe sore throat. Which response is best?

choices.text: Double the next methimazole dose
Continue without assessment for a month
Switch immediately to PTU without assessment
Treat with exercise alone
Withhold the drug and seek urgent CBC/evaluation

questions.explanation: The symptoms may signal agranulocytosis; withhold further doses pending urgent evaluation.

distractorExplanations.A: Increasing exposure is inappropriate.
distractorExplanations.B: This delays a potentially serious drug reaction.
distractorExplanations.C: A switch does not resolve the need to evaluate.
distractorExplanations.D: Exercise does not address the drug safety issue.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize antithyroid-drug agranulocytosis warning symptoms.

conditions.name: Thyroid nodule
conditions.overview: Study the initial evaluation of adult nodules using the ATA nodule recommendations, separate from differentiated thyroid cancer treatment.

sources.title: 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer: The American Thyroid Association Guidelines Task Force on Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer
sources.organization: American Thyroid Association; publisher-deposited full text in PubMed Central
sources.locator: Recommendations 2 and 6; Table 6 and recommendation 8: thyroid nodule evaluation (not differentiated cancer treatment)

sections.title: Initial assessment
sections.text: Measure TSH and perform thyroid/neck ultrasound for a suspected nodule; ultrasound pattern and size determine biopsy consideration.

sections.title: Low TSH changes the pathway
sections.text: Subnormal TSH prompts a radionuclide thyroid scan to assess function. Do not use that scan as the initial imaging choice when TSH is normal or elevated.

sections.title: High-suspicion ultrasound
sections.text: ATA recommends FNA for a high-suspicion nodule ≥1 cm. A solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications is an example of this pattern.

questions.stem: An adult has a newly detected thyroid nodule and subnormal TSH. Which additional test best evaluates whether the nodule is functioning?

choices.text: A radionuclide thyroid scan
Routine thyroglobulin as the sole test
A fasting lipid panel
A D-dimer
No evaluation because all nodules are malignant

questions.explanation: Subnormal TSH warrants radionuclide functional assessment in the ATA pathway.

distractorExplanations.B: It does not identify nodule function.
distractorExplanations.C: It does not evaluate thyroid function.
distractorExplanations.D: It does not evaluate thyroid function.
distractorExplanations.E: The premise is false and evaluation is still needed.

questions.learningObjective: Use TSH to select functional nodule imaging.

questions.stem: A euthyroid adult has a 1.4-cm solid hypoechoic thyroid nodule with microcalcifications. Which next diagnostic action best follows the ATA high-suspicion pathway?

choices.text: Ignore it because TSH is normal
Perform ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration
Repeat imaging only after ten years
Treat immediately with insulin
Use a normal TSH as proof of benign histology

questions.explanation: A high-suspicion nodule ≥1 cm meets the ATA FNA criterion.

distractorExplanations.A: Normal TSH does not establish benign histology.
distractorExplanations.C: That fails the indicated evaluation.
distractorExplanations.D: Insulin does not evaluate a thyroid nodule.
distractorExplanations.E: TSH does not establish histology.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the ATA high-suspicion nodule FNA threshold.

conditions.name: Obesity
conditions.overview: Study the 2025 federal approach to combined lifestyle, medication and procedural options.

sources.title: VA/DOD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Adult Overweight and Obesity
sources.organization: Department of Veterans Affairs and Department of Defense
sources.locator: Recommendations 2, 6–9, 12, 16–17; comprehensive lifestyle intervention and pharmacotherapy

sections.title: Combine lifestyle components
sections.text: A comprehensive intervention combines behavioral support, dietary changes and physical activity. An energy deficit supports weight loss; no single dietary pattern is universally preferred.

sections.title: Medication supplements lifestyle
sections.text: VA/DoD recommends semaglutide or tirzepatide with lifestyle intervention for BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with an obesity-associated condition, after assessing suitability and preferences.

sections.title: Plan long-term maintenance
sections.text: Weight maintenance needs ongoing support. The guideline supports continued pharmacotherapy to maintain achieved loss and considers metabolic surgery at BMI ≥35, or ≥30 with type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: An adult with BMI 34 wants a structured initial weight-management plan. Which program best reflects comprehensive lifestyle intervention?

choices.text: Diet advice alone with no follow-up
Only a promise of rapid weight loss
Behavioral support, dietary changes and physical activity
Avoiding all activity indefinitely
A supplement without assessment

questions.explanation: Comprehensive intervention combines behavioral, dietary and physical-activity components.

distractorExplanations.A: It omits two core components.
distractorExplanations.B: A promise does not constitute a program.
distractorExplanations.D: It omits physical activity.
distractorExplanations.E: It is not a comprehensive intervention.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the components of a comprehensive obesity intervention.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has BMI 28 and hypertension. Lifestyle support continues, and no contraindications to weight-management medicines are identified. Which option is supported by the 2025 VA/DoD guideline?

choices.text: Medicines are always prohibited below BMI 40
Replace lifestyle support entirely with medication
Prescribe thyroid hormone despite normal thyroid function
Consider semaglutide or tirzepatide alongside lifestyle intervention
Wait until a cardiovascular event occurs

questions.explanation: BMI ≥27 plus an obesity-associated condition meets the guideline category for these medications with lifestyle support.

distractorExplanations.A: That is not the guideline threshold.
distractorExplanations.B: The recommendation includes lifestyle intervention.
distractorExplanations.C: That is not the supported option here.
distractorExplanations.E: The recommendation does not require a prior event.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the medication eligibility category without treating it as a patient-specific prescription.

conditions.name: Stable coronary artery disease
conditions.overview: Study chronic coronary disease prevention, symptom management and testing decisions.

sources.title: Top Things to Know: 2023 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease
sources.locator: Items 3–7 and 10: exercise, antianginal treatment, statins and symptom-directed testing

sections.title: Secondary prevention
sections.text: Healthy eating, exercise and appropriate cardiac rehabilitation support chronic coronary disease care. Statins remain first-line lipid-lowering therapy.

sections.title: Treat angina and distinguish indications
sections.text: A beta blocker or calcium-channel blocker is first-line antianginal therapy. Long-term beta blockers are not recommended solely to improve outcomes without recent MI, LVEF ≤50% or another indication.

sections.title: Test for a clinical reason
sections.text: Routine periodic anatomic or ischemic testing is not recommended when clinical and functional status has not changed.

questions.stem: A patient with stable CAD has unchanged exercise capacity and no new symptoms since the previous visit. What is the best approach to routine annual ischemic testing?

choices.text: Order it automatically every year
Order it solely because of age
Replace all follow-up with imaging
Schedule urgent angiography despite no change
Avoid routine periodic testing without a clinical change

questions.explanation: Unchanged clinical/functional status does not warrant routine periodic ischemic testing.

distractorExplanations.A: Automatic testing is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.B: Age alone is not the stated indication.
distractorExplanations.C: Clinical follow-up still matters.
distractorExplanations.D: No change is supplied to justify that escalation.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid unnecessary surveillance testing in stable CAD.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic CAD has no MI in the past year, LVEF 60%, no angina and no other beta-blocker indication. Which statement best reflects the 2023 guideline?

choices.text: Routine long-term beta blocker is not recommended solely to improve outcomes in this scenario
All such patients require lifelong beta blockers solely for survival
Beta blockers replace statins
Exercise must be prohibited
Dietary supplements replace secondary-prevention medication

questions.explanation: The guideline distinguishes antianginal or other indications from unsupported routine outcome-only beta-blocker use.

distractorExplanations.B: The guideline does not make that blanket recommendation.
distractorExplanations.C: They do not replace lipid treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Activity is part of chronic disease care.
distractorExplanations.E: Supplements do not replace recommended prevention.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish beta-blocker indications in chronic coronary disease.

conditions.name: Acute coronary syndrome
conditions.overview: Study selected 2025 ACS management distinctions and secondary prevention.

sources.title: Top Things to Know: 2025 Guideline for Acute Coronary Syndromes
sources.locator: Items 1–2: DAPT default; item 6: cardiogenic shock culprit revascularization; item 9: rehabilitation

sections.title: Default antiplatelet strategy
sections.text: Aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor is the default DAPT strategy for at least 12 months in ACS without high bleeding risk; bleeding risk and anticoagulation can change the plan.

sections.title: Cardiogenic shock
sections.text: ACS with cardiogenic shock requires emergency culprit-vessel revascularization. Routine simultaneous PCI of non-infarct arteries is not recommended.

sections.title: Secondary prevention
sections.text: After discharge, referral to cardiac rehabilitation and follow-up lipid assessment are recommended; prevention continues beyond the acute procedure.

questions.stem: An adult completes PCI for ACS, has no high bleeding risk and no indication for chronic anticoagulation. What is the guideline default antiplatelet plan?

choices.text: No antiplatelet treatment after discharge
Aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor for at least 12 months
Aspirin only for two days in every case
An anticoagulant replaces both in every patient
Routine indefinite triple therapy for all

questions.explanation: The default is at least 12 months of DAPT when high bleeding risk is absent.

distractorExplanations.A: ACS needs antiplatelet management.
distractorExplanations.C: That is not the default duration or combination.
distractorExplanations.D: No anticoagulation indication is supplied.
distractorExplanations.E: Triple therapy is not the universal default.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the default ACS antiplatelet strategy and its stated exception.

questions.stem: A patient with acute MI develops cardiogenic shock and has a culprit artery plus additional nonculprit stenoses. Which strategy best follows the guideline?

choices.text: Delay revascularization until an outpatient appointment
Routine immediate PCI of every lesion regardless of culprit status
Emergency culprit-vessel revascularization without routine simultaneous nonculprit PCI
Treat only with dietary counseling
Use cardiac rehabilitation as the acute shock treatment

questions.explanation: Emergency culprit revascularization is indicated; routine simultaneous nonculprit PCI is not.

distractorExplanations.A: Shock requires urgent care.
distractorExplanations.B: The routine multivessel strategy is not recommended here.
distractorExplanations.D: Counseling does not treat acute shock.
distractorExplanations.E: Rehabilitation is a later prevention measure.

questions.learningObjective: Choose the revascularization focus in ACS with cardiogenic shock.

conditions.name: Heart failure
conditions.overview: Study ejection-fraction phenotypes, modern therapy classes and management after recovery.

sources.title: Top Things to Know: 2022 Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
sources.locator: Items 1–4, 7: GDMT including SGLT2 inhibitors; improved LVEF; evidence of elevated filling pressures

sections.title: Modern HFrEF therapy
sections.text: Guideline-directed HFrEF therapy includes four foundational medication classes, including an SGLT2 inhibitor. Therapy selection also depends on contraindications and tolerability.

sections.title: Improved EF does not erase history
sections.text: Patients with prior HFrEF whose LVEF improves above 40% should continue their HFrEF treatment rather than assume the disease is cured.

sections.title: Confirm preserved-EF disease
sections.text: When LVEF exceeds 40%, evidence of elevated filling pressures helps confirm heart failure. Natriuretic peptides, imaging and hemodynamic assessment may supply that evidence.

questions.stem: A patient previously had LVEF 30%. After treatment, LVEF is 52% and symptoms improve. What is the best medication principle?

choices.text: Stop all HFrEF treatment because EF normalized
Treat EF improvement as proof no heart disease ever existed
Continue only when edema returns
Continue HFrEF treatment if tolerated
Replace medication with supplements

questions.explanation: Improved LVEF after HFrEF is an indication to continue the HFrEF treatment plan.

distractorExplanations.A: Recovery does not justify blanket withdrawal.
distractorExplanations.B: Prior HFrEF remains relevant.
distractorExplanations.C: Treatment is not limited to episodes of edema.
distractorExplanations.E: Supplements do not replace GDMT.

questions.learningObjective: Maintain treatment after improvement of a previously reduced EF.

questions.stem: A patient has unexplained dyspnea and LVEF 60%. Which additional finding supports HFpEF rather than using normal EF alone to make the diagnosis?

choices.text: Only the absence of a murmur
A normal EF with no further evaluation
Normal shoe size
An isolated dietary preference
Evidence of elevated filling pressures

questions.explanation: With LVEF >40%, elevated filling-pressure evidence supports a heart-failure diagnosis.

distractorExplanations.A: That alone does not establish the diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.B: EF alone is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.C: It is not diagnostic evidence.
distractorExplanations.D: It is not diagnostic evidence.

conditions.name: Atrial fibrillation
conditions.overview: Study risk-based stroke prevention and anticoagulant exceptions.

sources.title: 2023 Guideline for Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation: Key Perspectives
sources.locator: Stroke prevention based on thromboembolic risk; DOAC exceptions; aspirin; lifestyle factors

sections.title: Stroke risk guides prevention
sections.text: Use a validated risk framework for estimated annual thromboembolism risk. At risk ≥2% per year, stroke prevention is based on that risk regardless of AF pattern.

sections.title: Choose the appropriate anticoagulant
sections.text: DOACs are preferred over warfarin for eligible patients, except with mechanical valves or mitral stenosis requiring a vitamin K antagonist.

sections.title: Aspirin is not a substitute
sections.text: In an anticoagulation candidate without another antiplatelet indication, aspirin alone or aspirin plus clopidogrel is not the recommended alternative for AF stroke prevention.

questions.stem: An adult with AF has an estimated annual thromboembolic risk above 2%, a mechanical mitral valve and no bleeding contraindication. Which anticoagulation option fits the guideline exception?

choices.text: Warfarin
Apixaban
Rivaroxaban
Dabigatran
Aspirin alone

questions.explanation: A mechanical valve is an exception to the usual DOAC preference; warfarin is appropriate.

distractorExplanations.B: A mechanical valve changes the usual DOAC choice.
distractorExplanations.C: A mechanical valve changes the usual DOAC choice.
distractorExplanations.D: A mechanical valve changes the usual DOAC choice.
distractorExplanations.E: Aspirin is not a substitute for indicated anticoagulation.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the mechanical-valve exception to DOAC preference.

questions.stem: A patient has paroxysmal AF and validated annual stroke risk above 2%. Renal function permits a DOAC, there is no mechanical valve or significant mitral stenosis, and there is no other antiplatelet indication. Which strategy best follows the guideline?

choices.text: Use aspirin alone because episodes are intermittent
Use an appropriate DOAC after shared decision-making
Prevent stroke only during symptomatic episodes
Use aspirin plus clopidogrel instead of anticoagulation
Ignore stroke risk if the office pulse is regular

questions.explanation: Stroke prevention follows thromboembolic risk regardless of AF pattern; eligible patients generally favor a DOAC.

distractorExplanations.A: AF pattern does not eliminate the risk-based indication.
distractorExplanations.C: That is not the recommended risk-based strategy.
distractorExplanations.D: Dual antiplatelets are not the recommended substitute.
distractorExplanations.E: A regular office pulse does not erase AF stroke risk.

questions.learningObjective: Base AF stroke prevention on risk rather than episode pattern.

conditions.name: Deep vein thrombosis
conditions.overview: Study probability-directed diagnosis and initial management of uncomplicated lower-extremity DVT.

sources.title: Diagnosis of Venous Thromboembolism: An Educational Slide Set
sources.locator: Lower-extremity DVT diagnostic strategies: pretest probability, D-dimer and ultrasound; avoid positive D-dimer as diagnosis

sources.title: Treatment of Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism: An Educational Slide Set
sources.locator: Initial anticoagulation; outpatient uncomplicated DVT; anticoagulation preferred over thrombolysis for most proximal DVT

sections.title: Start with probability
sections.text: Clinical pretest probability determines the diagnostic pathway. In low-probability suspected DVT, a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer can exclude DVT; otherwise ultrasound may be needed.

sections.title: A positive D-dimer is not confirmation
sections.text: Do not diagnose DVT from a positive D-dimer alone. Imaging confirms the diagnosis in the appropriate pathway.

sections.title: Most proximal DVT uses anticoagulation
sections.text: Most uncomplicated proximal DVT is treated with anticoagulation rather than routine thrombolysis. Suitable uncomplicated patients may receive outpatient treatment with appropriate support.

questions.stem: An ambulatory adult has low clinical pretest probability for a first lower-extremity DVT and a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer in an appropriate diagnostic pathway. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: DVT is confirmed
All patients require catheter venography
DVT can be excluded without additional testing in this pathway
Start thrombolysis solely from calf discomfort
A negative result confirms PE

questions.explanation: In a low-probability pathway, a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer can rule out DVT.

distractorExplanations.A: A negative result does not confirm DVT.
distractorExplanations.B: That is not required in this pathway.
distractorExplanations.D: There is no confirmed clot or indication for thrombolysis.
distractorExplanations.E: It does not confirm another clot diagnosis.

questions.learningObjective: Apply a low-probability DVT rule-out strategy.

questions.stem: Ultrasound confirms a first proximal leg DVT in a stable adult with mild symptoms, no limb threat and no anticoagulation contraindication. Which initial strategy is best?

choices.text: Routine systemic thrombolysis for every proximal clot
No treatment unless PE occurs
Aspirin alone as definitive treatment
Anticoagulation rather than routine thrombolysis
Place an IVC filter in every case

questions.explanation: Anticoagulation is preferred over routine thrombolysis for most uncomplicated proximal DVT.

distractorExplanations.A: The vignette lacks a reason for routine thrombolysis.
distractorExplanations.B: Confirmed proximal DVT needs treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: Aspirin is not the indicated initial strategy.
distractorExplanations.E: The vignette does not justify routine filter placement.

questions.learningObjective: Select standard initial therapy for uncomplicated proximal DVT.

conditions.name: Pulmonary embolism
conditions.overview: Study the 2026 PE severity framework, appropriate disposition and longer-term anticoagulation.

sources.title: Top Things to Know: 2026 Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism in Adults
sources.locator: Items 1–5: severity categories and hospitalization; item 8: oral anticoagulation; items 9–10: extended treatment and follow-up

sections.title: Assess severity rather than clot alone
sections.text: The 2026 AHA/ACC scheme spans categories A–E. Symptoms plus right-ventricular dysfunction or elevated biomarkers, incipient failure, or persistent hypotension warrant hospitalization.

sections.title: Oral anticoagulant selection
sections.text: For patients eligible for oral anticoagulation, a DOAC is recommended over a vitamin K antagonist unless contraindicated.

sections.title: Extended treatment and recovery
sections.text: Without a major reversible risk factor, or with a persistent risk factor, continued anticoagulation beyond the initial 3–6 months is recommended. Review symptoms and functional limitations for at least one year.

questions.stem: An adult has confirmed acute PE, dyspnea and right-ventricular dysfunction despite normal blood pressure. Which disposition best follows the 2026 severity guidance?

choices.text: Discharge automatically because BP is normal
Delay all treatment until a monthly visit
Treat as a category A asymptomatic PE
Ignore right-ventricular findings
Hospitalize to optimize management

questions.explanation: Symptomatic PE with right-ventricular dysfunction belongs to a category requiring hospitalization.

distractorExplanations.A: Normal BP does not eliminate elevated severity.
distractorExplanations.B: This delays necessary management.
distractorExplanations.C: The patient is symptomatic with RV dysfunction.
distractorExplanations.D: RV findings contribute to severity classification.

questions.learningObjective: Identify PE severity requiring hospitalization despite normotension.

questions.stem: A patient finishes initial anticoagulation for a first PE with no major reversible provoking factor. Bleeding assessment permits continued treatment. Which recommendation best fits the 2026 guideline?

choices.text: Continue anticoagulation into an extended phase after individualized discussion
Automatically stop at one month
Use aspirin as a universal replacement
Stop solely because symptoms resolved
Repeat only a chest radiograph instead of prevention

questions.explanation: Without a major reversible risk factor, extended anticoagulation is recommended after the initial phase.

distractorExplanations.B: That is shorter than the initial treatment phase.
distractorExplanations.C: It is not the stated replacement strategy.
distractorExplanations.D: Symptom resolution does not establish low recurrence risk.
distractorExplanations.E: A radiograph does not replace recurrence prevention.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a setting favoring extended PE anticoagulation.

conditions.name: Chronic kidney disease
conditions.overview: Study kidney damage/chronicity and kidney-protective therapy under international KDIGO recommendations.

sources.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
sources.locator: Practice points 1.1.1.1 and 1.1.3.1–2: GFR, ACR and chronicity; recommendations 3.7.1–2: SGLT2 inhibitors

sections.title: Demonstrate chronicity
sections.text: CKD requires persistent kidney-function or structural abnormalities for at least three months. One low eGFR during acute illness is insufficient to establish chronic disease.

sections.title: Use GFR and albuminuria
sections.text: Assess both eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio; they provide complementary information for staging and progression risk.

sections.title: Kidney-protective therapy
sections.text: KDIGO recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes with CKD and eGFR ≥20, and for eligible adults with CKD, eGFR ≥20 and ACR ≥200 mg/g or heart failure.

questions.stem: During an acute gastroenteritis episode, an adult has a first eGFR of 48. No prior renal records or chronic structural findings exist. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: CKD is established from this one value
Assess the acute cause and seek evidence of persistence/chronicity
This excludes any acute kidney problem
Classify permanent kidney failure immediately
Albuminuria testing is never useful

questions.explanation: A single low eGFR during acute illness does not establish the required chronicity.

distractorExplanations.A: Persistence or other chronic evidence is needed.
distractorExplanations.C: An acute cause remains possible.
distractorExplanations.D: The isolated value does not establish permanence.
distractorExplanations.E: ACR contributes to kidney assessment.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid diagnosing CKD from an isolated acute eGFR decrease.

questions.stem: A stable adult with type 2 diabetes has CKD, eGFR 38 and no contraindication to SGLT2 therapy. Which class is recommended for kidney protection?

choices.text: An antibiotic without infection
A benzodiazepine
SGLT2 inhibitor
A thyroid suppressant without thyroid disease
No kidney-protective consideration until dialysis

questions.explanation: KDIGO recommends an SGLT2 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes with CKD at eGFR ≥20.

distractorExplanations.A: There is no infection indication.
distractorExplanations.B: It is not the kidney-protective class.
distractorExplanations.D: It is not the kidney-protective class.
distractorExplanations.E: Kidney-protective treatment precedes dialysis.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the CKD SGLT2 recommendation at an eligible eGFR.

conditions.name: Acute kidney injury
conditions.overview: Study established KDIGO AKI definitions and urgent complications; the 2026 review draft is not treated as final guidance.

sources.title: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury
sources.locator: Recommendations 2.1.1, 2.3.1, 2.3.2, 5.1.1–2: diagnosis, cause assessment, monitoring and emergency renal replacement

sections.title: Recognize an acute change
sections.text: KDIGO AKI criteria include a creatinine rise ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, ≥1.5 times baseline within seven days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hour for six hours.

sections.title: Assess cause and trend
sections.text: Evaluate the cause promptly, including reversible contributors, and monitor creatinine and urine output; the clinical context matters beyond a single laboratory value.

sections.title: Renal replacement for complications
sections.text: Life-threatening fluid, electrolyte or acid-base abnormalities can require emergency renal replacement. Do not use an isolated BUN or creatinine threshold as the only trigger.

questions.stem: A hospitalized adult’s creatinine increases from 0.9 to 1.3 mg/dL in 36 hours. What is the best classification principle?

choices.text: No AKI because creatinine is below 2
CKD is proven solely by this change
AKI always requires anuria
This meets the acute creatinine-rise criterion for AKI
The increase can be ignored

questions.explanation: A 0.4-mg/dL rise within 48 hours exceeds the ≥0.3 AKI criterion.

distractorExplanations.A: The change criterion is not a fixed creatinine cutoff.
distractorExplanations.B: This is acute rather than proof of chronicity.
distractorExplanations.C: Creatinine or urine-output criteria can establish AKI.
distractorExplanations.E: The acute rise warrants evaluation.

questions.learningObjective: Identify AKI from the timing and magnitude of creatinine change.

questions.stem: A patient with AKI has refractory life-threatening electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities despite initial treatment. What best guides urgent renal replacement?

choices.text: Wait for creatinine to exceed a universal number
Wait until the next clinic visit
Use only the BUN value regardless of symptoms
Never provide renal replacement during acute illness
The life-threatening complications and overall clinical context

questions.explanation: Emergency renal replacement is guided by dangerous fluid, electrolyte or acid-base complications and context.

distractorExplanations.A: A single threshold is not the sole trigger.
distractorExplanations.B: The complications are urgent.
distractorExplanations.C: BUN alone is not the recommended decision rule.
distractorExplanations.D: Acute complications may require renal replacement.

questions.learningObjective: Use complications rather than an isolated laboratory cutoff for emergency renal replacement.

conditions.name: Nephrolithiasis

sources.title: Nutrition therapy for the prevention of kidney stones
sources.organization: CARI Guidelines; Australia and New Zealand
sources.edition: Date written October 2025; adult Australia–New Zealand guideline
sources.locator: Fluid intake recommendation a; volume-overload tailoring practice point; calcium recommendation c

sections.title: Confirm and look for obstruction
sections.text: Urine and blood testing plus appropriate imaging help identify stones and urinary blockage; symptoms alone do not determine stone size or location.

sections.title: Recognize need for urgent treatment
sections.text: Large stones, urinary obstruction or severe pain can require urgent treatment rather than waiting for spontaneous passage.

sections.title: Use stone-specific prevention
sections.text: Recovered stone analysis and selected 24-hour urine testing can guide recurrence prevention. Adequate liquids generally reduce risk, adjusted for comorbid fluid restrictions.

sections.title: Supplementary adult stone-prevention guideline
sections.text: Australia–New Zealand CARI guidance targets urine output ≥2.5 L/day with individualized fluid intake. Maintain normal dietary calcium for calcium stones; carefully tailor fluids when volume overload is possible.

questions.stem: An adult with flank pain has imaging-confirmed urinary obstruction from a large stone and severe uncontrolled pain. Which plan best fits the federal treatment reference?

choices.text: Urgent urologic assessment for treatment
Assume every stone passes safely without assessment
Wait six months regardless of pain
Treat only with a dietary supplement
Avoid evaluating obstruction

questions.explanation: Obstruction and severe pain are reasons stones may need urgent intervention.

distractorExplanations.B: Size and obstruction affect treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: The current findings warrant timely care.
distractorExplanations.D: A supplement does not address obstruction.
distractorExplanations.E: Obstruction is a key treatment factor.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize stone findings requiring urgent treatment assessment.

questions.stem: An adult with recurrent calcium stones has no fluid restriction. When studying supplementary Australia–New Zealand CARI guidance, which fluid goal is recommended?

choices.text: Stop drinking water after symptoms resolve
Individualize intake to achieve at least 2.5 L urine daily
Use the same fluid amount regardless of comorbidities
Aim for progressively more concentrated urine
Rely on calcium elimination instead of fluid planning

questions.explanation: CARI targets at least 2.5 L daily urine output; fluid advice is individualized, especially with volume-overload risk.

distractorExplanations.A: Recurrence prevention continues after symptoms resolve.
distractorExplanations.C: Comorbidities affect safe fluid planning.
distractorExplanations.D: Fluid intake aims to dilute urine.
distractorExplanations.E: CARI supports normal dietary calcium for calcium stones.

conditions.name: Uncomplicated cystitis

sources.title: Diagnosis of Bladder Infection in Adults
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: History, physical examination, urinalysis and urine culture

sources.title: Treatment for Bladder Infection in Adults
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: Medicines; unconfirmed diagnosis and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics; complicated bladder infections

sources.title: Outpatient Clinical Care for Adults
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Acute uncomplicated cystitis: healthy adult nonpregnant premenopausal women; first-line agents and fluoroquinolone reservation

sections.title: Evaluate a lower urinary syndrome
sections.text: Use history, examination and urine testing to assess suspected bladder infection. Urinalysis can show inflammatory findings; culture identifies bacteria and can inform treatment.

sections.title: Use antibiotic information appropriately
sections.text: When bacterial bladder infection is supported, antibiotic choice considers the organism and drug allergies. If the diagnosis is unconfirmed, evaluate alternatives rather than assuming antibiotics are always needed.

sections.title: Recognize upper-tract illness
sections.text: Progression to kidney infection changes assessment and treatment; severe illness can require intravenous antibiotics and hospital-level care.

sections.title: Use scoped federal antibiotic recommendations
sections.text: For healthy nonpregnant premenopausal adults with uncomplicated cystitis, CDC lists nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin and TMP-SMX when local resistance is <20% as first-line options. Reserve fluoroquinolones when other agents are unsuitable.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old nonpregnant woman has culture-confirmed cystitis. The organism is resistant to her empiric antibiotic. Which plan best supports the next antibiotic selection?

choices.text: Continue the initial drug regardless of resistance
Assume every antibiotic has identical activity
Use susceptibility results and the drug-allergy history
Choose a drug that caused a previous serious allergy
Avoid antibiotics in every confirmed bacterial bladder infection

questions.explanation: Organism susceptibility and allergy history guide an effective, suitable antibiotic.

distractorExplanations.A: Resistance is a reason to reassess selection.
distractorExplanations.B: Susceptibility results distinguish antibiotic activity.
distractorExplanations.D: The allergy history must affect selection.
distractorExplanations.E: Confirmed bacterial infection may warrant antibiotics.

questions.learningObjective: Use susceptibility and allergy information to select targeted cystitis treatment.

questions.stem: A healthy 27-year-old nonpregnant woman has uncomplicated cystitis, normal kidney function and no drug allergies. Which plan matches CDC first-line recommendations?

choices.text: Choose a fluoroquinolone routinely before suitable alternatives
Avoid all antibiotics despite confirmed bacterial infection
Choose TMP-SMX regardless of local resistance
Use an appropriate first-line agent such as nitrofurantoin
Treat every case as a hospitalized kidney infection

questions.explanation: Nitrofurantoin is a first-line option within this population; fluoroquinolones are reserved when other agents are unsuitable.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC reserves fluoroquinolones when alternatives are unsuitable.
distractorExplanations.B: Confirmed bacterial infection warrants appropriate treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC conditions TMP-SMX use on local resistance <20%.
distractorExplanations.E: The vignette describes uncomplicated lower-tract infection.

questions.learningObjective: Apply federal first-line cystitis recommendations within the defined adult population.

conditions.name: Pyelonephritis

sources.title: Diagnosis of Kidney Infection (Pyelonephritis)
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: Urinalysis; urine culture; blood tests; imaging for abnormalities and obstruction

sources.title: Treatment for Kidney Infection (Pyelonephritis)
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Urinary Tract Infections

sections.title: Assess infection and kidney function
sections.text: Urinalysis and urine culture support diagnosis; culture identifies bacteria. Blood tests assess serious infection and kidney function, and imaging may identify structural problems.

sections.title: Adjust antibiotics to results
sections.text: Antibiotics are started for kidney infection and may be changed when laboratory results identify the organism. Severe illness may require hospitalization and intravenous treatment.

sections.title: Address structural contributors
sections.text: A urinary blockage or structural problem may need procedural correction in addition to antibiotics; antibiotic treatment alone does not remove a mechanical obstruction.

sections.title: Monitor complicated infection response
sections.text: CDC includes pyelonephritis among complicated UTIs and recommends close monitoring for treatment failure. Presentation may require hospitalization; antimicrobial susceptibility patterns affect treatment planning.

questions.stem: An adult is treated for pyelonephritis. The urine culture later identifies an organism resistant to the initial drug. What is the best next principle?

choices.text: Continue the inactive drug because treatment already began
Stop reviewing all microbiology
Replace antibiotics with exercise
Assume cultures never affect treatment
Change to an effective antibiotic guided by laboratory results

questions.explanation: Laboratory identification and susceptibility results can require antibiotic adjustment.

distractorExplanations.A: Resistance makes reassessment necessary.
distractorExplanations.B: Results should inform treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: Exercise does not replace infection treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Cultures can change treatment selection.

questions.learningObjective: Adjust pyelonephritis therapy using culture results.

questions.stem: A patient with kidney infection has a urinary blockage identified on imaging. Which plan best addresses both problems?

choices.text: Evaluate and correct the blockage while treating the infection
Antibiotics alone always remove the blockage
Ignore imaging once antibiotics begin
Treat only the blockage and ignore infection
Defer assessment for a year

questions.explanation: Obstruction may require procedural treatment in addition to antibiotics.

distractorExplanations.B: Antibiotics do not mechanically remove obstruction.
distractorExplanations.C: Structural findings affect treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Both infection and obstruction need attention.
distractorExplanations.E: The identified complication needs timely care.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize the need to address obstruction with upper urinary infection.

conditions.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
conditions.overview: Study evaluation and medication mechanisms from a federal reference; current AUA2026 recommendations remain a separately identified rights/access gap.

sources.title: Enlarged Prostate (Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia)
sources.organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.locator: Diagnosis; watchful waiting; alpha blockers and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors; treatment escalation

sections.title: Evaluate symptoms and alternatives
sections.text: History, examination and urine testing help assess lower urinary tract symptoms. Review medication contributors and how symptoms affect quality of life.

sections.title: Mild unbothersome symptoms
sections.text: Watchful waiting with follow-up can be appropriate when enlargement and symptoms do not meaningfully affect quality of life.

sections.title: Distinguish drug mechanisms
sections.text: Alpha blockers relax bladder-neck/prostate smooth muscle; 5-alpha reductase inhibitors reduce prostate growth or size. Combination therapy may benefit selected patients.

questions.stem: An older adult has mild BPH symptoms that do not affect quality of life, with no identified complication. Which option is reasonable?

choices.text: Immediate prostate surgery for everyone
Watchful waiting with follow-up
Indefinite antibiotics without infection
Chemotherapy as the default
Ignore symptoms permanently with no reassessment

questions.explanation: Watchful waiting is an option for mild, unbothersome symptoms.

distractorExplanations.A: The vignette does not require immediate surgery.
distractorExplanations.C: No infection is identified.
distractorExplanations.D: BPH is not an indication for default chemotherapy.
distractorExplanations.E: Watchful waiting includes follow-up.

questions.learningObjective: Choose observation for mild unbothersome BPH symptoms.

distractorExplanations.A: This class targets growth/size through a different mechanism.

conditions.name: Gout
conditions.overview: Study crystal disease and guideline-based urate-lowering treatment principles.

sources.title: Gout
sources.locator: Signs and symptoms; joint fluid diagnosis; Common Treatments

sources.title: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout
sources.locator: Tables 1–3 and flare management: tophi/frequent flares, allopurinol first line including CKD, serum urate <6 mg/dL, prophylaxis 3–6 months

sections.title: Separate urate elevation from gout
sections.text: High serum urate alone does not prove gout. Joint-fluid assessment for urate crystals may clarify a swollen-joint diagnosis.

sections.title: Choose and titrate therapy
sections.text: For gout warranting urate-lowering treatment, ACR prefers allopurinol first line, including CKD. Start low, lower in CKD, and titrate using serial urate toward <6 mg/dL.

sections.title: Prevent initiation-related flares
sections.text: When starting urate-lowering treatment, anti-inflammatory prophylaxis is recommended for at least 3–6 months, adjusted for ongoing flares and individual medication risks.

questions.stem: An adult with recurrent gout and tophi has CKD stage 3 and an indication for urate-lowering therapy. No contraindication to allopurinol is identified. Which approach best follows ACR?

choices.text: Never use allopurinol in CKD
Start the maximum dose immediately
Use pegloticase as routine first-line therapy
Begin allopurinol at a low dose and titrate to urate target
Use diet alone as the mandatory sole therapy

questions.explanation: Allopurinol remains preferred first line in CKD, with low-dose initiation and titration.

distractorExplanations.A: CKD does not exclude the preferred first-line agent.
distractorExplanations.B: High-dose initiation is not recommended.
distractorExplanations.C: Pegloticase is not first-line therapy.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated disease warrants pharmacologic consideration.

questions.learningObjective: Apply allopurinol first-line therapy safely in gout with CKD.

questions.stem: A patient begins indicated urate-lowering therapy after recurrent gout flares. Which accompanying plan best follows ACR?

choices.text: No prophylaxis because a urate drug prevents every early flare
Stop prophylaxis after a single day regardless of flares
Avoid monitoring urate permanently
Stop urate therapy whenever the laboratory value improves
Anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for at least 3–6 months with reassessment

questions.explanation: Prophylaxis during initiation reduces flare risk and continues at least 3–6 months with reassessment.

distractorExplanations.A: Early flares remain possible.
distractorExplanations.B: That is shorter than the recommended interval.
distractorExplanations.C: Serial urate informs titration.
distractorExplanations.D: A brief improvement does not justify this blanket stop rule.

questions.learningObjective: Use anti-inflammatory prophylaxis when starting urate-lowering therapy.
